# Part 1: Autogenerated documentation as a context base

Status: agreed on 2026-08-28.

## Goal

Work on many projects at the same time without the agent rediscovering each project from scratch.
Documentation is the context mechanism: it is input to every task and also part of its output.
The convention belongs to Sebastian, not to the project.
Every project (new or existing) adapts to the same structure, so that a single set of skills works across all of them without adaptation.

## Principles

1. Do not document what the code already says; document the why.
   What can be derived from the code (columns, types, request/response) is generated from the source of truth and is not copied into Markdown.
   The intentional part (product, decisions, debt, invariants) is written by the agent when each task finishes.
2. Progressive disclosure.
   The agent reads little at the start and digs deeper only into what it needs.
   Loading all the documentation upfront degrades the agent as much as having none at all.
3. Documentation stays fresh through the workflow, not through hooks.
   Every change goes through the skills, and the skills have the documentation step as mandatory.
   Pre-commit hooks or automatic blocks will not be used for this (an explicit decision).
4. Inferred content is marked.
   When the agent infers something without evidence (for example, the why behind a decision in an old project), it marks it with `[inferido]` so Sebastian can confirm or remove it.
   Without this marker, invented decisions would end up treated as truth.

## Document types

### PRD (Product Requirements Document)

Describes what the system does and why, without engineering detail.
It exists at a general level and at a module level (scoped and more specific).
It is edited in place: it reflects the current state of the product, it does not accumulate history.

### TRD (Technical Requirements Document)

Describes how the system is built.
It exists at a general level and at a module level.
It is edited in place: it reflects the current technical state.

The general TRD declares the stack and its mechanics.
This includes how API specs are generated, how tests, lint and migrations are run.
The skills read this section to know how to operate in the project, instead of having one skill per stack.

The module TRD includes the list of endpoints the module owns, one line per endpoint with its purpose and a link to the generated spec.
Request/response is not duplicated in Markdown.

### ARD (Architecture and Debt Record)

Records architecture decisions and technical debt.
It exists at a general level (global decisions and a debt index) and at a module level.

Unlike the PRD and the TRD, the ARD is a log.
Each decision is a new, dated entry.
Old entries are not deleted; at most they are marked as superseded by a later entry, or as having had their debt resolved by a task.
The value of the ARD lies in the trail, not just in the final state.

Each ARD entry contains:

- Date.
- Decision made.
- Alternatives discarded.
- Reason for the choice.
- Technical debt it generates (if applicable), and the task that later paid it.
- Trigger to revisit it (for example, "when there are more than N tenants" or "when we migrate to X").

### database.md (per module)

Describes the module's impact on the database.
Contains:

- Tables the module owns.
- Tables from other modules it references.
- Invariants that live only in code and are not enforced by the database.

It does not copy columns or types.
The source of truth for the schema remains Prisma, TypeORM, migrations, or the stack's equivalent.

### flows.md (per module, only if applicable)

State and sequence diagrams for complex flows.
They are written in Mermaid inside the Markdown: it is text, it is versioned with git, the agent reads and edits it like code, and it renders on GitHub.
Only for flows that warrant it; a diagram for a CRUD is noise.

### API specification

Generated from the code, not written by hand.
Examples: `@nestjs/swagger` in NestJS, rswag or the GraphQL schema in Rails.
The general TRD indicates how it is generated in each project.
The agent reads the generated JSON or schema when it needs request/response detail.

## File structure

Centralized in `docs/` instead of alongside the code, so it works the same way in NestJS, Next.js, Rails and React Native.
The agent always knows where to look regardless of the stack.

```
CLAUDE.md                  # short: stack, commands, and "the docs live in docs/"
docs/
  PRD.md                   # general product
  TRD.md                   # general technical, declares stack and mechanics
  ARD.md                   # global decisions + index of open debt
  conventions/             # optional: one rule per file, when TRD Conventions is not enough (i18n, style)
  checks/                  # optional: review checks the om-reviewer runs per round (see below)
  modules/
    {{module}}/
      README.md            # 20-40 lines: what it does, boundaries, links to the rest
      prd.md
      trd.md               # includes endpoints it owns
      ard.md               # module log
      database.md
      flows.md             # mermaid: states and sequences (only if applicable)
```

### Review checks (`docs/checks/{{name}}.md`, optional)

A check is a small, single-rule review the om-reviewer delegates to a cheap model in the background on every round: i18n coverage, a style the linter cannot express, a module's patterns.
Frontmatter: `name`, `model` (bare alias, usually `sonnet`), `paths` (globs relative to the project root, repo folder first in multirepo; the check runs only when the diff touches a matching file), `reference` (the document that defines the rule).
Body: verifiable statements in the present tense, one per line, and a closing line saying what to report as clean.
No reference document, no check: the rule must be written in `TRD.md` Conventions, a module's `trd.md` or `docs/conventions/{{topic}}.md` before the check exists.
Checks are added with `add-check` by the om-manager on Sebastian's ask; the om-reviewer triages their output and only verified lines reach the om-developer.

## Versioning

Git is the versioning system; no manual changelog is built inside each file.

Since the git author is always Sebastian even when an agent writes the commit, each document carries a minimal frontmatter:

```yaml
---
updated: 2026-08-28
source: 0142_badge_wall   # the task that caused the change
---
```

This solves traceability (which task changed this decision) and detection of stale documents (an old `updated` in an active module is a sign of drift).

## Agent reading path

1. `CLAUDE.md`: short, points to the project's documentation structure.
2. `docs/PRD.md` and `docs/TRD.md`: general context of the product and the system, and the list of modules.
3. Decide which module the change makes sense in.
4. Reads in depth only that module: `README.md` and then whichever files it needs.

This way the agent does not fill up with all the information, only what is necessary.

## Skills

A single set of skills, generic in its flow.
Stack-specific detail does not live in separate skills, but in two places:

- The project's general TRD, which declares stack and mechanics.
- `references/{{stack}}.md` files inside the skill, loaded only if detail is needed.

Adding a new stack means adding a reference file, not a skill.
This replaces the four current copies of `implement-specs-*` (nestjs, nextjs, rails, react-native) with a single `execute-task`.

| Skill | Role |
|---|---|
| `setup` | Creates or reconciles the documentation convention in a project. Calls `write-prd`, `write-trd` and `write-ard`. |
| `plan-task` + `create-task` | Planning phase. Reads the documentation following the reading path and produces the task folder on disk. |
| `execute-task` | Implements the task. Operates according to the stack declared in the TRD. When the review is clean, calls `document-task` once. |
| `document-task` | Updates the PRD, TRD, ARD, database and flows of the touched module, with `updated` and `source`, once per task, when the code is final. |
| `review-task` | Verifies that the task touched what was necessary; the documentation check happens in `publish-task`. |

The complete list of skills by role is in [03-skills.md](03-skills.md).

### setup

It is unique and idempotent.
It works for empty repos, old repos with no documentation, and half-done repos.
Conceptually it always does the same thing:

1. Detects the state: stack, existing modules, which documentation exists and which is missing or stale (based on `updated`).
2. Produces a gap report: ideal state vs. current state.
3. Fills the gaps by calling `write-prd`, `write-trd` and `write-ard`, at the general level and per module.
   Inferred content is marked with `[inferido]`.
4. Writes or adjusts the short `CLAUDE.md`.

In an old project, step 3 is heavy and is parallelized per module with clean-context subagents.
In a new project it is nearly instant.

### document-task

It must be a named, mandatory step, run once per task or phase, on the om-reviewer's clean signal and before publish.
If it is not explicit, the agent skips it when the context gets long.
Updates:

- `prd.md` and `trd.md` of the module: edited in place.
- `ard.md` of the module: new entry with decisions made and debt generated, and `Resolved by` on the entries whose debt this task paid.
- `ARD.md`: its debt index, and only that, so it bills open debt and not work already done.
- `database.md` and `flows.md` if the change affects them.
- `updated` and `source` frontmatter on each touched file.

### publish-task

As a second line of freshness, it checks before pushing: does the touched module have its documentation up to date?
